Couple featured in Netflix documentary

NEW DELHI: A Russian couple who went viral after scaling the Empire State Building in New York and unfurling a banner carrying a message of love and peace before an apparent marriage proposal could face deportation from the US after a plea deal with prosecutors fell through.Angela Nikolau, 33, and Ivan Kuznetsov, 32, appeared in a New York criminal court on Thursday (November 12), where their lawyer said an agreement to plead guilty to misdemeanour charges had been withdrawn. Nikolau was seen tearing up during the hearing as the possibility of deportation emerged.The couple had reportedly been negotiating a deal with prosecutors that would have allowed them to avoid what their lawyer described as serious immigration consequences. However, according to Fox News, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office withdrew the offer through an email sent the night before the hearing."We didn't damage any property. We didn't intend to put anyone in danger. We just wanted to send a message of love, and we're ready to defend ourselves," Kuznetsov told reporters."We wanted to share a message of peace. With so much pain in the world today, we wanted to create a performance to stay in the people's hearts," Nikolau added.Noam Biale, the couple's attorney, said his team had accepted an offer from prosecutors for the pair to plead guilty to misdemeanour charges in exchange for protection from what he called "catastrophic immigration consequences".The deal, however, was taken off the table shortly before the hearing."If sent back to Russia, Mr Kuznetsov will almost certainly be sent to fight in the war in Ukraine and Ms Nikolau may be jailed for her artistic expression," Biale said.The couple, originally from Moscow, were charged with felony reckless endangerment, burglary and other offences following their climb in July. Their lawyer's latest comments have raised concerns over the potential immigration consequences of the criminal proceedings.The incident took place on July 2, when Nikolau and Kuznetsov climbed the Empire State Building's broadcast antenna, reaching a height of around 1,454 feet (443 metres) above Manhattan.After reaching the top, they unfurled a black banner carrying the message: "When the power of love beats the love of power the world knows peace".Kuznetsov then proposed to Nikolau on a ledge slightly below the antenna's peak. The couple later shared pictures of the stunt on social media.According to the criminal complaint, police found a broken lock on a security door on the building's restricted-access 104th floor, which provides access to the antenna. The highest floor open to visitors is the 102nd-floor observation deck.Police waited for around half an hour for the antenna to be powered down before officers from the Emergency Services Unit began climbing the structure. They eventually intercepted the couple as they were making their way down.Authorities said the unauthorised climb also put responding officers at risk, with personnel required to ascend to around 1,250 feet (381 metres).The Empire State Building's management described the climb as unauthorised.Nikolau and Kuznetsov, who also goes by the name Ivan Beerkus, are known for climbing skyscrapers and other tall structures, often without authorisation.Their relationship and rooftop-climbing exploits were featured in the 2024 Netflix documentary Skywalkers: A Love Story. The film followed the couple as they undertook dangerous climbs of tall buildings and explored their relationship.The documentary premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2024.
Article Summary: Angela Nikolau, 33, and Ivan Kuznetsov, 32, appeared in a New York criminal court on Thursday. Their lawyer said an agreement to plead guilty to misdemeanour charges had been withdrawn. Nikolau was seen tearing up during the hearing as the possibility of deportation emerged.

Article Title: In 1944, 19-year-old Marine Henry Keen recorded a July 4 message for his family at a Hollywood USO; killed at Iwo Jima eight months later, it remains his only known recording
Article Text:
AI Representation: Marine Henry Keen recorded a July 4 message for his family at a Hollywood USA, killed at Iwo Jima eight months later. Image credits: Chatgpt

A message recorded at the Hollywood USO

Eight months later, Keen was killed at

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Iwo Jima

Raising the flag on Iwo Jima. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A short recording made at a Hollywood USO in 1944 preserved something a family could never expect to lose: the sound of their son's voice. According to the Mississippi Armed Forces Museum, on July 4, that year, 19-year-old Marine Henry L. Keen recorded a personal message for his mother in Braxton, Mississippi. He spoke about life in Hollywood, asked whether his father had been fishing and told his mother she could expect him home around the fourteenth. The recording remains the only known audio recording of him. The Mississippi Armed Forces Museum preserves the recording and publishes its full transcript, offering a rare glimpse into the everyday thoughts of a young Marine during World War II Keen’s message was part of a wartime project called “Voices of Victory,” produced by GEM Razors and Blades. The project allowed military personnel to record personal messages for relatives waiting at home. According to the Mississippi Armed Forces Museum, these messages were stored on lacquered cardboard discs that families could keep and play. Keen was stationed in California when he visited the Hollywood USO on Independence Day 1944.A woman introduced the recording by addressing his mother, Mrs. Keen, in Braxton, Mississippi. She explained that the message was from the Hollywood USO before handing the recording over to him.Keen began by greeting his family and joking about being in “good old LA” before correcting himself to “Hollywood”. He said he was having a good time and hoped everyone at home was doing well. He also asked about his father, wondering whether he had been fishing. The young Marine mentioned that he was with a couple of friends. He described the USO as a welcoming place with free food, drinks, music, records and an orchestra. His message sounded relaxed, with casual remarks about his surroundings and the people he was spending time with. He told his family that they could expect him home around the fourteenth and imagined himself knocking at the door. Near the end, a woman prompted him to tell his mother that he loved her. Keen initially said goodbye, but after another prompt, he added, “Love y’all. Son.” The original audio recording preserved these small details, including his pauses, jokes and affectionate sign-off.It was not the reunion Keen had envisioned. According to the Mississippi Armed Forces Museum archives, PFC Henry L. Keen was killed in action at Iwo Jima only eight months later from the time when the recording was made. The Battle of Iwo Jima occurred in February-March 1945 and was a part of the Pacific Theatre operations during World War II. It was a bloody battle, one of the costliest battles for the Americans during the war. There is no information provided by the museum about the details of Keen’s death. All that is known is that he died in the Battle of Iwo Jima and left behind his recording of July 1944.As stated in the museum, the July 4 disc is the only recording of Keen that survived. Unlike a picture or military service record, the recording offered more than proof that he existed, because he was speaking directly to his mother. There was nothing extraordinary in the message that lacked any rhetoric about the war and prediction of the future. The disc only held a teen talking about his friends, eating, listening to music, fishing and coming back home.
Article Summary: Marine Henry L. Keen was stationed in California when he visited the Hollywood USO on July 4, 1944. Keen recorded a personal message for his mother in Braxton, Mississippi. He spoke about life in Hollywood, asked whether his father had been fishing and told his mother she could expect him home around the fourteenth. The recording remains the only known audio recording of him.

Article Title: In an Iowa gravel-road trial, engineers buried a layer made with recycled plastic; it raised bearing capacity by up to 30%, boosted stiffness 25% and cut moisture in the road base by 10-20%
Article Text:
AI Representation: Engineers buried a layer made with recycled plastic in Iowa gravel-road trial. Image credits: Chatgpt

How recycled plastic became part of the road base

Field trials showed improvements and road strength

Could the system reduce

road construction costs

?

A close-up view of a gravel road. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A composite geosynthetic system incorporating recycled plastic could help strengthen Iowa’s gravel roads and reduce moisture in their foundation. During full-scale field trials in Buchanan County, engineers found that the system increased road bearing capacity by up to 30%, improved stiffness and elastic modulus by 25% and reduced moisture in the road base and subgrade by 10% to 20%. This research provided a possible solution not only for recycling plastics, but also for the betterment of the rural road structure in the state. According to Iowa State University’s report, Iowa has more than 71,000 miles of gravel county roads. Although these roads typically carry low traffic volumes, they routinely handle heavy loads from farm equipment, construction vehicles and service trucks, making their maintenance important for rural communities. Weather conditions, along with the wear and tear caused by heavy traffic, tend to deteriorate their condition.The experiment was conducted by researchers from the Program for Sustainable Pavement Engineering and Research (PROSPER) at Iowa State University. They came up with the idea of creating a composite geosynthetic system consisting of a geogrid made of 100% recycled plastic and a nonwoven geotextile joined together.Geogrids are grids used for reinforcement in the construction of roads and other structures. According to Iowa State University’s College of Engineering, the researchers 3D printed the geogrid using a filament made entirely from recycled plastic. The research had been partially funded by the Iowa Department of Transportation and Iowa Highway Research Board. It represented an integral part of extensive research on alternative recycled materials used for building roads. Another source of the material is wind turbine blades.Three full-scale test sections were built in Buchanan County to evaluate various methods of reinforcement. One section utilised the recycled plastic composite geosynthetic, the other one involved the use of an analogous geosynthetic but made from virgin plastic and the third one was the control, reinforced test section. The test sections were subjected to a range of conditions, including truckloads, agricultural operations and different seasons of the year. Their performance was assessed using Light Weight Deflectometer testing, California Bearing Ratio testing, rut depth determination, sand cone density testing and moisture and temperature sensors.The results were published in January 2026 in the Journal Transportation Geotechnics in the article Field Performance of Recycled and Virgin Plastic Composite Geosynthetics in Gravel Roads: Moisture Mitigation and Structural Advantages. As a result of its use, the bearing capacity of the road structure increased by up to 30%, which meant that it would be capable of handling heavier loads. In addition, there was a 25% increase in stiffness and elastic modulus, which implied higher resistance to deformation under loads. There was a decrease in moisture content of the road base and subgrade soils by 10 to 20%.The results of the study could be significant in the context of constructing and maintaining roads in rural areas. Enhanced reinforcement enabled engineers to use a thinner layer of granular base without compromising its effectiveness. This resulted in using less aggregate while constructing the roads. The research project also includes analysing the cost efficiency of the system. Further monitoring is still needed so that scientists can evaluate the long-term performance of the material.According to Iowa State University’s PROSPER project information, the research began on March 1, 2022 and is scheduled to continue through August 31, 2027. The test done in Buchanan County indicates that the use of recycled plastic composites may have the ability to improve the road structure while finding an additional application for waste products. Further studies in the field will help identify whether this method may be applied to other roads in Iowa. The project is formally listed as 22-792, TR-799, with Halil Ceylan as principal investigator and Sunghwan Kim as co-principal investigator.Its six tasks run from material characterisation and laboratory assessment through pilot test sections, cost-effectiveness evaluation and practitioner guidance, with the work intended to produce best practice recommendations for Iowa’s gravel road network.
Article Summary: Engineers at Iowa State University created a geogrid made of 100% recycled plastic and a nonwoven geotextile. The system increased road bearing capacity by up to 30%, improved stiffness and elastic modulus by 25% and reduced moisture in the road base and subgrade by 10 to 20%.

Article Title: In 1943, US Sgt. Cody Wolf recorded a Christmas message in England that mentioned his baby daughter; he was killed weeks later, and she heard his voice as an adult 70 years later
Article Text:
A 1943 Christmas broadcast brought a father’s voice home, though it took 70 years to reach his daughter (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

A black box in a newspaper library

Old records, new meaning: A forgotten broadcast reached the daughter it named seven decades later (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

A father's message from England

Hearing her own name

From a silent movie to a voice

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Margaret Ann Wolf Harris never really imagined what her father's voice sounded like. Sgt. Cody Wolf was killed in World War II when his plane was shot down over Germany on 11 January 1944. She was just 17 months old. In December 2013, she heard him speak, at age 71, according to an NPR report published by South Carolina Public Radio. It was the first time she had heard his voice. The voice came from a Christmas radio show in 1943, found in the paper’s library by a newspaper researcher.Researcher Paul McCardell was browsing through the library of The Baltimore Sun when he found a black box secured by rope. It contained vinyl records. Steve Sullivan, a multimedia editor, described it as a pristine copy of a 1943 radio show. The Poynter Institute , summarising reports from The Sun, stated that the two records were each 30 minutes long. They copied the Christmas broadcast from 25 December 1943, sponsored by The Sunpapers. The program was broadcast from two bases in England, with help from the Army Special Services and the BBC. The program had messages from the soldiers, airmen, and Red Cross workers. McCardell and Sullivan wanted it back on the radio, to be heard by the world once more, so they reached out to Sun columnist Dan Rodricks, who also hosted a show on WYPR.The station aired the broadcast on 20 and 24 December 2013.That Christmas, more than 50 service members and aid workers sent messages home. One of them was Sgt. Cody Wolf. Wolf told the broadcaster that he had been thinking a lot about Catonsville, Maryland. When asked if he had a family there, he named his parents, his wife and, in his own words, “my 16-month-old daughter, Margaret Ann”. Rodricks thought the broadcast was charming and a little chilling. The men were six or seven months away from the invasion of Europe, and many had flown several bombing missions over Germany. Later, Harris explained, no one had expected her father to be on the show. It was only a few weeks since he had come to England. The broadcast went out on Christmas Day, and he was killed in action on 11 January 1944.A friend who heard the show live on WYPR told Harris to look for it online. She said it didn't register until she heard his voice. She then emailed Sullivan and McCardell. She told them she was Sgt. Wolf's daughter, that she had heard her father's voice for the very first time, and they had sent her a precious Christmas present. In her NPR interview, Harris recalled the moment as not sad at all. She said it was a wonderful experience. The “most poignant part”, she added, was hearing her dad say her name. She described his voice as calm and reassuring, typical of his family and of the time. She compared it to the voices of Jimmy Stewart and Gary Cooper. Her daughters and grandchildren heard it, too.Harris is a retired teacher. According to Poynter’s 20214 report, citing The Sun, she continues to live in the home of her grandparents on Prospect Avenue, where she moved together with her mother after her father went into service.She said that she had all the photos and memorabilia, but they were “like a silent movie”. Now she has his voice. For years, radio has been a way of sending Christmas greetings over long distances. This one brought a father’s message to a daughter decades later. The Library of Congress says that shortwave broadcasting let Christmas programmes be broadcast around the world. As the 1930s wore on, even festive broadcasts could not ignore world events. Wolf's wartime message was rescued from a box, broadcast, and eventually found its way to the daughter he named on air.
Article Summary: Margaret Ann Wolf Harris heard her father's voice for the first time in December 2013. Sgt Cody Wolf was killed in World War II when his plane was shot down over Germany on 11 January 1944. The voice came from a Christmas radio show in 1943, found in the paper’s library by a researcher.

Article Title: Watch: Passengers jump into water as luxury ship collides with tanker on Mississippi River
Article Text:
A freighter collided with a cruise ship carrying around 130 people in New Orleans, causing the paddlewheel vessel to capsize. More than 30 people were hospitalized.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A video emerged showing the American Heritage river cruise ship sinking into the Mississippi River in New Orleans after colliding with the Atlantic Asphalt tanker on Friday. Passengers can be seen panicking and jumping into the water as the five-storey vessel begins to tilt and eventually goes down.Rescue teams, including tugboat operators, dock workers and police personnel, rushed to the scene to pull people from the river.All passengers and crew aboard the cruise ship were rescued, with no one reported missing. At least 32 people were taken to hospital, but none suffered critical injuries, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said. Around 180 people, including passengers and crew, were aboard the vessel when the tanker struck it at the Port of New Orleans.The American Heritage began taking on water and listing sharply within minutes of the collision, triggering a large-scale rescue operation. Dozens of people were pulled from the water, including at least two police officers.The tanker apparently lost steering before crashing into the docked cruise ship."We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said at a news conference, as rescuers and others cheered.“It was docked right at the Port of New Orleans when a tanker ship lost control and collided into the cruise ship,” Moreno said.The American Heritage began listing within minutes of the collision and eventually flipped while emergency personnel were still working to evacuate those aboard.Dozens of passengers and at least two police officers were pulled from the Mississippi River, where the water temperature was around 19 degrees Celsius.Devon Flanagan, who was working nearby at the Port of New Orleans, said he saw workers rushing towards the dock before noticing that the cruise ship had overturned and passengers were struggling in the water.“It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.”The exact cause of the collision remains unclear. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of loss of steering”.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) was expected to investigate the incident. However, its investigators were initially unable to reach New Orleans after flights across the country were grounded due to communication problems at regional air traffic control centres.Passengers who were not injured were taken to a nearby auditorium, where cruise officials conducted a roll call to ensure everyone was accounted for, Moreno said.Many passengers lost their identification documents and car keys during the incident. Most were visitors from outside New Orleans and needed assistance with accommodation, transportation and other basic arrangements.“They needed chargers for their phones. Some people didn't have phones,” Moreno said. “This has now made national news. They need to contact their families to let them know they're OK. Food, hotel rooms, transportation.”The American Heritage, operated by American Cruise Lines, was completing an eight-day voyage covering several destinations along the Mississippi River in Louisiana and Mississippi.Built in 2015, the 160-metre-long vessel can accommodate up to 150 passengers. It was scheduled to end its journey in New Orleans, according to maritime tracking website MarineTraffic.Martin Davies, a maritime law expert at Tulane University, said it was too early to establish the cause of the collision. However, videos of the incident appeared to indicate a possible catastrophic failure of systems aboard the tanker.He described the circumstances as “super bad luck” because the collision occurred as passengers were departing the cruise ship.Davies said the tanker was travelling upriver against the current at a relatively slow speed.“For something like this to happen for an upbound ship indicates that something must have gone really badly wrong,” Davies said.He added that tankers generally have local pilots aboard to guide them through waterways because of their familiarity with the river and the vessel. The tanker had also completed the difficult Algiers Point turn on the Mississippi River before the collision.According to the International Maritime Organisation, the tanker is owned by Nave Shipping SA, a company registered in Monrovia, Liberia. MarineTraffic identifies it as a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a major Chinese state-owned conglomerate.The corporation accounted for nearly a quarter of the global commercial shipbuilding market in 2022 and was also the world's largest military shipbuilder at the time, according to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.China State Shipbuilding Corporation did not respond to an emailed request for comment on Friday afternoon.During his first term, US President Donald Trump listed the corporation among more than two dozen Chinese-owned companies that he accused of exploiting “United States investors to finance the development and modernisation” of the Chinese military.The executive order did not freeze all economic transactions involving the listed companies but imposed restrictions on the types of transactions they could undertake on US soil.The Atlantic Asphalt specialises in transporting large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid petroleum-based material commonly used in road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.
Article Summary: Around 180 people, including passengers and crew, were aboard the paddlewheel vessel. At least 32 people were taken to hospital, but none suffered critical injuries. The American Heritage began taking on water and listing sharply within minutes of the collision. Dozens of people were pulled from the water, including two police officers.

Article Title: In 2015, Arizona engineers buried geogrid beneath a forest road; five years later, reinforced sections had no ruts or potholes, while untreated soil deteriorated
Article Text:
A forest road in northern Arizona, shown with and without the buried mesh that helped it hold up (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

Why this road needed help

Geogrid, a strong mesh, is laid over the soil before the aggregate layer goes on top (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

What the engineers built

What the road looked like five years on

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

What it proves and what it doesn't

Anyone who has bounced along a rough country road would probably know how fast mud, ruts and potholes can ruin a journey. Engineers in northern Arizona tried a quiet fix on one such road back in 2015. A 2023 Geotechnics paper by Chun-Hsing Ho, Jeremy DeGeyter and Dada Zhang followed that fix for five years. Engineers installed a strong mesh called geogrid beneath a Forest Service road near Marshall Lake, south and east of Flagstaff. By 2020, the strengthened sections had no ruts or potholes, but the untreated soil next to them kept getting worse.The test site was selected for a reason. The road already had deep ruts, and there was proof of failure of another fabric installed in the past. This road provided access to one section of the Arizona Trail, which was closed down by the Forest Service during winter months. Conditions on this road were especially difficult. Flagstaff sits at an elevation of 2,250 metres above sea level. The authors explained that there were around 200 to 250 freeze-thaw cycles annually, along with lots of snow in winter and summer monsoons. The soil beneath was a weak clay with some sand in it. They noted that forest officers have limited budgets. As a result, maintaining unpaved roads was difficult. Geogrids were considered for trial as they would reduce both maintenance and construction costs.The team built four test sections along a 40-metre stretch, each 4.3 metres wide and 10 metres long. The geogrid was inserted between the soil and a layer of aggregate, a gravel-like material used to build roads. Three of the sections had geogrids, one with 15 centimetres of aggregate and two with 30 centimetres, while the fourth had 30 centimetres but no geogrid. The work was done in November 2015, just before a winter storm hit northern Arizona. Next to the four plots, the team left one section of plain native soil as a control. The design software indicated that unreinforced ground required 33 centimetres of aggregate to achieve the target strength, while a section with geogrid required only 15 centimetres. Stiffness testing post-build showed the native soil scored 73.9 megapascals, while the best reinforced section scored as high as 390.7 megapascals. The native soil settled under the test load to 15.77 millimetres instead of 2.1 to 3.5 millimetres in the geogrid sections.By May 2020, no rutting and pothole distress was noted in the reinforced sections. However, the control section had a much different experience. The researchers observed rutting, potholes and cracking in the control section, and these were increasing over time.Moreover, the team drove a sensor-equipped vehicle over all five sections to measure how bumpy each one felt. The untreated soil’s average smoothness score was 0.040 centimetres. The two best sections, 30 centimetres of aggregate with geogrid, gave scores of 0.010 and 0.011. A 15-centimetre geogrid section scored at 0.021, outperforming a 30-centimetre section without geogrid at 0.030.A similar pattern was seen by researchers at Oregon State University on a test road in western Oregon. A 2016 study in the European Journal of Forest Engineering by Erica Kemp, Ben Leshchinsky and Kevin Boston found that geogrid on native soil prior to the placement of aggregate reduced pressure on the soil during loading. It also reduced rutting with well-graded aggregate. Still, the Arizona result is from one road in one place. The Arizona team called for more research on aggregate thickness and drainage. Several backers, including the geogrid supplier, supported the project. So geogrid isn't a cure-all, but in this test, a buried layer helped support the road over the five-year study period.
Article Summary: Engineers installed a strong mesh called geogrid beneath a Forest Service road near Marshall Lake, south and east of Flagstaff. By 2020, the strengthened sections had no ruts or potholes, but the untreated soil next to them kept getting worse. A similar pattern was seen on a test road in western Oregon.

Article Title: In 1945, Sgt. Seymour Silverman mailed a coconut from Guam to his one-year-old daughter in Virginia; he drew on it, coated it in shellac and wrote her address on the shell
Article Text:
Representative image of a coconut sketched on, sealed in shellac and addressed by hand. Image Credits: ChatGPT

Life on Guam after the fighting

The National Museum of American Jewish Military History in Washington, DC, which shares the stories of Jewish service members, including Sgt. Seymour Silverman. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

How a coconut became a parcel

A daughter who followed him into uniform

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why small things matter

Most of us probably know what it feels like to miss someone and want to send them something that shows it. One American soldier in 1945 found a very strange way to do it. In the Summer 2010 issue of The Jewish Veteran , news from the National Museum of American Jewish Military History in Washington, DC, reported that Sgt. Seymour Silverman mailed a coconut from Guam to his one-year-old daughter in Virginia. He drew on the coconut, coated it in shellac, and wrote her address on the shell. The shell itself worked as the package.In 1944, Guam saw fierce and bloody battles with the Japanese forces, just like most of the Pacific battles during the time. The magazine explained that by 1945, the island was already a peaceful place for the soldiers, sailors, and marines serving there. There was no longer any fear of an attack from the Japanese even before V-J Day. Servicemen could enjoy palm-lined beaches, lovely scenery and entertainment from the USO and Red Cross. However, none of these was important to Silverman, who was serving with the 355th Bomb Squadron. He desperately wanted to return to his wife and daughter. He was drafted into the Army in 1942, and his daughter was born in 1944.Silverman was seeking a way to feel close to his family. He picked the coconut from a palm tree and drew a picture on it.Then he covered it in shellac, wrote the home address on the outside and dropped it straight into the mail. No box was required. The fruit was both a gift and an envelope. The coconut was addressed to his one-year-old daughter, Marita, and travelled from an army airfield on the island to the family home in Portsmouth, Virginia. The article suggested he might have felt less lonely thinking about his little girl with it in her hands. The coconut also linked his life in Guam to his family at home.However, the story didn't end there. The same article revealed that Marita went on to become an Army officer herself. Records from the University of Maryland School of Nursing show that Marita Silverman was part of its class of 1966. She became an Army Nurse Corps officer and arrived in Vietnam in August 1970 as a first lieutenant assigned to the 125-bed 8th Field Hospital in the Central Highlands. In November 1970, she transferred to the 95th Evacuation Hospital in Da Nang, where she was promoted to captain. The little girl who received the coconut on the other side of the world grew up to serve abroad like her father had in a different war.A coconut might be an odd keepsake, but it tells a very human story. War history is usually told in terms of battles and big dates. Objects like this coconut show a quieter side where a homesick father, unable to be at home, sends the peace of the island where he was stationed to his daughter. According to the museum, the coconut still holds the emotion of a man doing his duty, but wishing he could share his life with his family. Today it helps the museum to tell the story of one service member. Little things like this can make history feel personal, not distant. The coconut shows how something simple can hold love across the ocean.
Article Summary: Sgt. Seymour Silverman mailed a coconut from Guam to his one-year-old daughter in Virginia. He drew on the coconut, coated it in shellac, and wrote her address on the shell. The coconut was addressed to his daughter, Marita, and travelled from an army airfield on the island to the family home in Portsmouth.

Article Title: Meet Mary Engle Pennington, denied a university degree because she was a woman, who went on to transform America’s food safety standards and revolutionise the refrigeration of milk, eggs and meat.
Article Text:
PC; US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)

How did Mary Engle Pennington break barriers in science education

How did Mary Engle Pennington improve food safety through refrigeration

How did Engle Pennington overcome gender discrimination at the FDA

How did Pennington transform food preservation in America

How did Pennington transform refrigerated railway transport

How did Pennington's inventions transform food preservation

What awards and honours did Mary Engle Pennington receive

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mary Engle Pennington faced barriers to studying science simply because she was a woman, but went on to become one of America's leading food safety pioneers. After her request to study chemistry was rejected by her school's headmistress, she pursued higher education at the University of Pennsylvania, where women were not awarded degrees at the time. She eventually earned a doctorate in chemistry in 1895 and became the first woman to head the Food Research Laboratory in 1906. Her research transformed the preservation, refrigeration, storage and transportation of perishable foods, helping establish food safety standards across the United States.Pennington's interest in science developed when she was just 12 years old. After borrowing a copy of Rand's Medical Chemistry from her local library, she became fascinated by the subject. She subsequently asked the headmistress of the private girls' school she attended to introduce a chemistry course. However, her request was rejected because the headmistress believed chemistry was not a subject for girls or women.According to the National Inventors Hall of Fame, Pennington continued pursuing her scientific interests despite the restrictions placed on women's education at the time. When she turned 18, she enrolled at the University of Pennsylvania, where she studied chemistry and biology.In 1892, she received a certificate of proficiency in the subjects because the university did not award degrees to women at the time. Her academic performance, however, was sufficiently impressive for the university to admit her to a graduate programme. She earned her doctorate in chemistry in 1895.After completing her doctorate, Pennington faced difficulties finding employment. According to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), she established the Philadelphia Clinical Laboratory, where she began conducting bacteriological analyses. One of her early areas of work involved improving the safety of ice cream sold to schoolchildren. She worked to educate farmers about the proper handling of raw milk to help improve the quality of the milk supply.In 1905, Pennington joined the US Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Chemistry. The FDA's historical account states that Harvey Wiley, who headed the Bureau of Chemistry, began working with her on cold-storage problems that year. Her research focused on understanding how refrigeration could help preserve food and prevent bacterial growth. This work became particularly important following the passage of the Pure Food and Drugs Act of 1906, which established a framework for federal regulation of food and drugs.In 1906, Pennington was allowed to apply for the position of chief of the Bureau of Chemistry's Food Research Laboratory. She was initially hesitant because she understood that being a woman could affect her chances of securing the position. However, Wiley encouraged her to take the civil service examination and submitted the hiring request using the name "M.E. Pennington" to conceal her gender.Pennington achieved the highest possible score in the examination and was offered the position. She became the first woman to serve as the FDA's laboratory chief in 1906. The FDA's historical account also describes how Wiley defended her appointment after her gender became known, arguing that civil service law did not permit her exclusion simply because she was a woman.Following the passage of the 1906 Pure Food and Drugs Act, Pennington's laboratory worked on research that improved the handling and preservation of perishable foods. Her work helped demonstrate that fresh foods could remain usable for longer when maintained at consistently low temperatures. Eliminating temperature fluctuations helped keep bacterial counts low in refrigerated foods, including eggs, milk and cheese.As chief of the Food Research Laboratory, Pennington also developed standards for the safe processing of chicken and procedures to reduce bacterial contamination in milk. She researched methods of storing and transporting poultry, eggs and other perishable products without spoilage. The National Inventors Hall of Fame records that her methods were subsequently adopted across the food-handling industry.When the United States entered World War I in 1917, Pennington was assigned to the War Food Administration (WFA), an agency associated with future President Herbert Hoover. Its work focused on maximising food production and conservation during the war.One of her responsibilities involved testing the storage and cooling systems of the country's 40,000 refrigerated railway cars. She experimented with different loading racks, ice bunkers and circulation systems to improve the distribution of cold air throughout the carriages. Her research helped establish national standards for ice-cooled refrigerator cars, including standards for their construction and insulation. She also worked on addressing humidity-control problems in cold storage.Pennington emphasised the importance of conserving food during wartime. In a 1917 letter to the St. Louis Railway Club, she wrote: "We are at war…we need food…and that food must be saved." Her work on refrigerated transport contributed to efforts to improve the storage and movement of food supplies across the country.Pennington's work also resulted in several patented inventions. According to the National Inventors Hall of Fame, these included a poultry-cooling rack, a bacteria-resistant method of treating eggs and a sterile container for food products. Her research covered different stages of food preservation, from processing immediately after harvesting or catching to storage and transportation.She also developed an efficient process for scaling, skinning, quick-freezing and dry-packing fish fillets immediately after they were caught. Later in her career, she oversaw the design and construction of both commercial and domestic refrigerators. These projects extended her work beyond government research into the development of refrigeration equipment for wider use.In 1919, Pennington left government service to continue working on food preservation. According to the FDA, she subsequently developed an interest in the safety of frozen foods, which became a major focus in the later years of her professional career.Her contributions received recognition from scientific and professional organisations. In 1940, she received the Garvan Medal from the American Chemical Society. In 1947, she was elected a fellow of the American Society of Refrigeration Engineers, where she served on committees and contributed to the organisation's publications. She was also recognised as an authority on the handling, transportation and storage of perishable foods.Pennington died on December 27, 1952, aged 80. In 1959, she became the first woman inducted into the American Poultry Historical Society Hall of Fame. Much later, in 2018, she was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame for her contributions to food preservation and storage. Her work on refrigeration, food safety and the transportation of perishable products helped shape practices used throughout the American food supply system.
Article Summary: Mary Engle Pennington studied chemistry at the University of Pennsylvania. She became the first woman to head the Food Research Laboratory in 1906. Her research transformed the preservation, refrigeration, storage and transportation of perishable foods. She helped establish food safety standards across the United States.

Article Title: In 1944, a US paratrooper left his fiancée’s letters in Belgium; 66 years later, the box returned to the couple, who had married in 1946
Article Text:
A wooden box of wartime letters waited 66 years to come home (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

Why letters mattered, and a surprise in the attic

For decades, the box sat quietly in an attic in Belgium (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

A race to bring it home

.

The kitchen table moment

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Imagine losing a box of your most treasured messages, then getting it back on a random day decades later. That's what happened to John Alfred D’Amore and his wife, Rose, according to a United Service Organisations (USO) story. John was 21 in 1944, a private first class in Headquarters Company, 82nd Airborne Division. There were no barracks, so he lived with a local family in Nandrin, Belgium, where he kept a hand-carved wooden box filled with letters from his fiancée, Rose Archie, as well as photos of friends and fellow soldiers. He hoped to carry it back home one day. Instead, he ended up in hospital with a broken ankle and never went back to the house, so the box remained where he had left it. John returned home safe and sound. On 29 June 1946, he and Rose got married in Niagara Falls, New York. They later had two children, two grandchildren, and two great-grandchildren.Letters were a lifeline for soldiers in those times. In a Library of Congress article about wartime correspondence, it is explained that letters and telegrams were virtually the only way to communicate between service members and civilians. The letters provided comfort for those enduring loneliness and fighting in war.News from home, or the lack thereof, could have had a major impact on morale. Hence, Rose’s letters meant much more than just a piece of paper; they were her voice, close at hand in terrifying times. Then in early June 2011, Anne-Marie Radelet, a Belgian lady, was cleaning up the attic of her late father-in-law when she discovered the box. It had a name and a place of origin on its cover. Realising that somebody had lost their memories, she gave it to the Ardennes American Cemetery employee. The American Battle Monuments Commission places the cemetery near Neupré, 12 miles southwest of Liège.The cemetery's superintendent, Alan Amelinckx, read some of the letters for clues, then searched online for the name on the box, but found nothing. He then called the city clerk in Niagara Falls, and after a few more phone calls, he got John's son, John David D’Amore. The real surprise came next: John and Rose were alive and living in Florida near their son. But there was one problem. Amelinckx was not able to cover the postage with government funds. He thought the box should be returned to the family. He recalled a family he had taken on a tour around the cemetery the summer before. Their father, Gerald Leary, was the regional president for Europe, the Middle East, the Indian subcontinent, and Africa for FedEx. Leary had offered help if ever needed. Amelinckx called him, and a FedEx courier picked up the box that same dayThe day of delivery saw the family waiting at John David's house for the FedEx van. The two veterans stepped out of the van and carried the box inside. About 15 people sat down in the kitchen while John David unpacked the box and laid out the contents: letters, several 82nd Airborne patches and ribbons and wartime photographs. John looked at the pictures he had taken and, while his short-term memory was impaired, he remembered names, places and situations, from driving entertainers Marlene Dietrich and Bob Hope to landing behind enemy lines in a glider.Rose recognised the card, and pictures she had sent him and her first comment, as her son recalled, was that she hoped she hadn't said anything bad. Only a few weeks later, the couple celebrated their 65th wedding anniversary. John David plans to keep the box in the family so the history will not be forgotten. The story can be a gentle reminder that some keepsakes are worth saving, and perhaps worth passing on to someone who will be glad of them one day.
Article Summary: A wooden box of wartime letters waited 66 years to come home. John Alfred D’Amore and his wife, Rose, were alive and living in Florida. Letters were a lifeline for soldiers in those times. John David plans to keep the box in the family so the story will not be forgotten.

Article Title: The Trump administration has proposed selling parts of America's federal land holdings to states, tribes and local governments under a new five-year plan, but has not identified which parcels could be
Article Text:
The plan prioritises energy production, critical minerals, AI infrastructure and restructuring federal wildfire management operations.

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the Trump administration's proposal to transfer federal land management to state and local authorities? Yes, it will improve efficiency No, it could restrict public access 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

America's vast public landscapes, long regarded as a shared national inheritance, are once again at the centre of a political battle over who should control the country's natural resources. President Donald Trump 's administration has outlined a proposal that could reshape the future of federally managed land, opening the door to sales and transfers to states, tribal governments and local authorities. While officials have presented the move as an effort to improve efficiency and redirect resources towards conservation, the absence of clearly identified properties and disposal criteria has raised concerns among conservationists, outdoor enthusiasts and lawmakers.A new direction for federal land managementAccording to The Washington Post, the proposal forms part of a five-year strategic plan released by the Department of the Interior, outlining the agency's priorities for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. The 28-page document identifies four central objectives, including reducing the size of the federal estate by offering certain properties for purchase to states, local governments and tribes.The department has argued that disposing of lands considered less nationally significant would allow it to concentrate resources on properties of greater federal importance. However, neither the specific parcels under consideration nor the geographical scope of potential sales has been disclosed. The administration has also not explained what qualifies a property as nationally significant, the report adds.According to The Washington Post, the Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles of land, an area larger than Texas and California combined, alongside extensive underground mineral resources. Much of this estate is concentrated in Western states, where federal ownership remains particularly substantial. Nevada, for instance, has nearly 80 per cent of its territory under federal control.Under the proposed arrangement, some proceeds from land sales would be returned to purchasing entities for conservation initiatives elsewhere, potentially supporting improved recreational access while reducing the government's long-term management expenses.Conservationists raise access concernsThe proposal has drawn criticism from outdoor recreation groups concerned that transferring federal properties to state authorities could eventually restrict public access. Outdoor Life reports that hunting and fishing advocates are particularly worried about losing access to lesser-known Bureau of Land Management properties that remain important recreational destinations.The distinction between federal and state ownership is significant. State-managed properties often operate under different access regulations, with restrictions on camping, driving and recreational activities. Consequently, a transfer could make certain landscapes less accessible even if they remain publicly owned.Outdoor Life also highlights concerns about the department's proposed workforce consolidation. The strategic plan promises further reductions across federal agencies, including the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management and US Fish and Wildlife Service. These organizations have long struggled with staff and funding, raising concerns about their ability to meet current needs.The only areas identified for potential staffing expansion are law enforcement and public safety, rather than conservation operations.Legal, political oppositionBipartisan opposition exists to the proposal. The former Trump interior secretary told The Washington Post that Ryan Zinke still opposes selling public lands. He has indicated that he would vote against legislation advancing such a move.Democratic lawmakers have also pledged to resist the initiative, arguing that federally owned landscapes should remain protected from commercial interests. Their opposition follows earlier unsuccessful attempts by some Western lawmakers to sell large portions of federal land, including a proposal by Utah Republican Senator Mike Lee involving more than two million acres.Legal restrictions could present another obstacle. Natural resources law professor Mark Squillace told The Washington Post that federal legislation places significant limits on property disposals. Protected lands cannot simply be sold, while other parcels must satisfy specific requirements, such as being uneconomical to manage or supporting important public objectives, including community expansion and economic development.Wider changes to public land policyThe strategic plan extends beyond property sales. Outdoor Life reports that it also prioritises domestic energy production, critical mineral development, artificial intelligence infrastructure and a major restructuring of federal wildfire management through a new US Wildland Fire Service.Separately, the Bureau of Land Management has proposed changes to its resource management planning process. The proposed rule would eliminate the existing 90-day public comment period for major plans and remove the requirement to release draft plans for public feedback, potentially replacing these processes with public meetings. The proposal remains open for public comments until January 11, 2027.These changes could have considerable implications because BLM resource management plans help determine where activities such as mining, drilling and grazing are permitted, as well as which properties may be considered for disposal.Although the five-year strategy establishes the administration's direction, it does not guarantee that the proposed land transfers will happen. Congressional approval and existing federal protections remain important considerations. For now, with no specific parcels identified, the proposal has opened a wider debate about whether America's public lands should primarily serve economic development, conservation or the millions of people who rely on them for recreation.Images Courtesy: istock and Instagram
Article Summary: The proposal forms part of a five-year strategic plan released by the Department of the Interior. The plan prioritises energy production, critical minerals, AI infrastructure and restructuring federal wildfire management operations. The proposal has drawn criticism from outdoor recreation groups concerned that transferring federal properties to state authorities could restrict public access.

Article Title: A California beach town facing disappearing sand and repeated disruption to a coastal railway voted down a proposed tax that could have raised $15 million a year, leaving officials to find another way
Article Text:
A costly battle against coastal erosion

Nearly 690,000 cubic yards of sand planned

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Officials face difficult funding decisions

San Clemente, a coastal city in Southern California known for its beaches and surfing culture, is facing a growing financial challenge as years of shoreline erosion threaten public beaches, coastal infrastructure and a railway connecting San Diego with the rest of the state. Residents have rejected a proposed tax increase that could have generated approximately $15 million annually for beach restoration and wildfire prevention, leaving city officials to reconsider how they will pay for long-term protection. According to reports by SFGATE, Voice of OC and LAist, nearly two-thirds of voters opposed Measure M in the November 3, 2026, election. The proposal would have increased the city's sales tax by one percentage point, taking it from 7.75% to 8.75%. The additional revenue was expected to support two dedicated funds over a 10-year period, with half allocated to beach protection and the remaining half directed towards wildfire preparedness. The measure was defeated despite growing concerns about the city's shrinking coastline and the repeated disruption of passenger and freight rail services along the coastal corridor.The erosion problem has become particularly serious around San Clemente's southern shoreline, where powerful waves and high tides have repeatedly threatened railway tracks.The route is an important transportation link between San Diego and other parts of California, but sections have faced closures as the coastline has deteriorated. The loss of sand has also affected beaches farther north. In some areas, erosion has become severe enough to threaten public access and city infrastructure. The city previously spent approximately $800,000 on a sand replenishment project in 2024 to protect its beach and safeguard the lifeguard headquarters near the pier.San Clemente has explored several ways to slow the damage, including installing large rocks along vulnerable sections of the coastline and constructing seawalls. However, these approaches have raised concerns about restricting public beach access and potentially shifting erosion to other parts of the shoreline.Sand replenishment has emerged as another important option, although it requires substantial investment and repeated maintenance. The city has already undertaken several such projects, but the volume of sand needed to maintain its beaches continues to grow.The financial challenge has become more urgent following a series of extreme weather events. The recent Norte Fire, which started in the hills above the city, forced thousands of residents to evacuate and destroyed seven homes. This added another layer of pressure to the proposed tax, which was designed to address both coastal erosion and wildfire risks. The defeat of Measure M follows another unsuccessful attempt to secure dedicated funding for beach restoration. A similar sales tax proposal was rejected by voters in 2024, although the earlier measure faced a different approval threshold.Despite the election setback, some immediate coastal protection work is moving forward. The Orange County Transportation Authority (OCTA) secured approval from the California Coastal Commission on November 5 for a major sand replenishment and railway protection project. According to OCTA, the plan involves placing approximately 690,000 cubic yards of sand along San Clemente's coastline. The project includes 450,000 cubic yards at San Clemente State Beach and another 240,000 cubic yards around North Beach and Mariposa Point.The approved plan also includes additional shoreline protection measures intended to stabilise the railway corridor and reduce the risk of further service disruptions. The Coastal Commission's approval provides a route for the work to proceed, although it does not resolve the city's wider funding requirements. However, the planned sand placement is largely tied to protecting the railway and does not establish a permanent funding arrangement for maintaining all of San Clemente's public beaches.With voters rejecting the proposed tax, city officials will have to consider redirecting existing funds or pursuing other sources of financial support. A regional approach involving coastal communities from Los Angeles to San Diego has also been suggested, potentially allowing municipalities to share the costs of large-scale sand replenishment and equipment such as dredgers.Another possibility is bringing a revised tax proposal before voters in the future, particularly if erosion worsens during the coming storm season. The failed measure has highlighted the difficulty of balancing the rising costs of coastal protection with residents' concerns about higher taxes. For San Clemente, the immediate challenge is no longer simply finding enough sand to restore its beaches, but securing the money needed to keep them from disappearing.
Article Summary: Nearly two-thirds of voters opposed Measure M in the November 3, 2026, election. The measure was defeated despite growing concerns about the city's shrinking coastline. The city has explored several ways to slow the damage, including installing large rocks along vulnerable sections of the coastline and constructing seawalls.

Article Title: Suicide car bombing at security checkpoint in Pakistan kills 5, injures 13

At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, a security official reported on Friday.The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district, along the N-25 national highway. Article Summary: At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province. Article Title: Pakistani teen mauled to death by tigress released from cage for TikTok video shoot
Article Text:
Pakistani teenager mauled to death after tigress freed for TikTok video in Lahore (Image source: X)
